common_names: redwood (European trade name for Scots pine)
region: Northern Hemisphere natively; radiata pine widely planted in the Southern Hemisphere
description: Pine is the most common construction and furniture softwood, including eastern white pine, southern yellow pines, Scots pine, and plantation radiata pine. It is used for framing, shelving, furniture, mouldings, and pallets, and many pines are resinous.

hazards.summary: IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancer of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long-term heavy exposure. This applies to every species, so dust control matters whatever you cut.

A small share of Danish furniture workers had IgE antibodies to pine dust, more often those with asthma, and a German carpenter's softwood allergy (spruce, pine, larch) was confirmed by skin and challenge tests. Allergy to pine protein appears uncommon.

The UK HSE lists a decrease in lung function for pine. New Zealand sawmill studies of radiata pine found more asthma symptoms, cough, and nose and eye irritation, and lower lung function at higher dust levels.
Eye irritation was more common in New Zealand pine sawmill workers with higher exposure. This is a survey finding, not a confirmed allergy.

effects: airborne dermatitis of face and hands
hazards.summary: Pine resin contains colophony (rosin) and abietic acid, common skin allergens. Finnish and Australian patients reacted on patch testing to pine sawdust and colophony, and a German case followed contact with untreated pine furniture.
The UK HSE lists skin irritation as a reported effect of pine dust, across many pine species.

effects: skin reaction made worse by sunlight
hazards.summary: The UK HSE notes that pine may cause photosensitisation, meaning skin reacts more strongly after sun exposure. We did not find a primary paper on this for pine.
A Finnish report described allergic alveolitis (lung inflammation) linked to pine sawdust. Only the title is available on PubMed, so the testing and whether mold was involved are not confirmed.

exposure_limits.note: 8-hour time-weighted average, as restated by OSHA

related_species_note: Hoop pine (Araucaria) and 'Huon pine' are not Pinus. Colophony is also present in spruce and other softwoods. In European trade 'redwood' can mean Scots pine; California redwood (Sequoia) has its own page.

notes_internal: Genus entry. Evidence sources by species: Skovsted-2003 'pine' (Danish furniture industry, species not stated in abstract); Kespohl-2012 softwood mix with spruce dominant; Douwes-2001/2006 New Zealand pine sawmills (radiata pine is the NZ plantation species, but the abstracts just say pine); Cook-1997 Pinus radiata; Estlander-2001 Finnish pine or spruce (Scots pine likely, not stated); Booken-2006 untreated pine furniture. Malmstrom-1999 alveolitis has no abstract; sawmill alveolitis is often mold-related, so flagged. Colophony asthma from soldering flux is not a wood-dust exposure and was excluded. Spiewak 1994, Kersten 1994, Dutkiewicz 2001 (from Schlunssen-2018) not checked. Image prompt uses eastern white pine as representative; common_names includes the European trade sense of 'redwood' for search. Absence of reports for a hazard is not evidence that this wood is safe.
